paragraphs: I have shown how democracy destroys or modifies the various inequalities that arise in society. But is that all? Does it not in the end also affect that great inequality of man and woman, which until today has seemed to rest eternally on human nature? I believe that the social changes that bring father and son, master and servant, and superiors and inferiors in general closer to the same level will raise woman as well, and make her more and more the equal of man. But here, more than ever, I feel the need to make myself clearly understood, for there is no subject on which the coarse and lawless fancies of our age have ranged more freely.

There are people in Europe who confuse the distinct characteristics of the sexes and would make man and woman not merely equal but alike. They would give both the same functions, lay on both the same duties, and grant both the same rights; they would mix them together in everything: their occupations, their pleasures, their business. It is easy to see that by trying to make one sex equal to the other in this way, one degrades both; and from so absurd a jumble of nature’s works nothing could ever come but weak men and disorderly women. This is not how the Americans understand the kind of democratic equality that may be established between the sexes. They admit that, since nature has set such wide differences between the physical and moral constitution of man and woman, her evident design was to give their various faculties distinct employments. They hold that improvement does not lie in making beings so unlike do nearly the same things, but in getting each of them to carry out their own tasks as well as possible. The Americans have applied to the sexes the great principle of political economy that governs the manufactures of our age: they carefully divide the duties of man from those of woman, so that the great work of society may be better carried on.

In no country has such constant care been taken as in America to draw two clearly separate lines of action for the two sexes and to have them keep pace with each other, but on paths that are always different. American women never manage the family’s outside affairs, or run a business, or take part in political life. Nor, on the other hand, are they ever forced to do the rough labor of the fields or any of those heavy tasks that demand physical strength. No family is so poor as to be an exception to this rule. If an American woman cannot escape the quiet circle of domestic occupations, neither is she ever forced to go beyond it. So it is that the women of America, who often show a masculine strength of understanding and a manly energy, generally keep great delicacy of personal appearance and always keep the manners of women, although they sometimes prove that they have the hearts and minds of men.

Nor have the Americans ever supposed that one consequence of democratic principles is the overthrow of marital power or the confusion of the natural authorities within the family. They hold that every association must have a head if it is to achieve its purpose, and that the natural head of the conjugal association is the man. They therefore do not deny him the right to direct his partner. They maintain that in the small association of husband and wife, as in the great social community, the object of democracy is to regulate and legitimize the powers that are necessary, not to overthrow all power. This opinion is not held by one sex and disputed by the other. I never observed that the women of America regard conjugal authority as a fortunate usurpation of their rights, or that they thought themselves degraded by submitting to it. It seemed to me, on the contrary, that they take a kind of pride in the voluntary surrender of their own will, and make it their boast to bend to the yoke rather than shake it off. Such at least is the feeling expressed by the most virtuous of their sex; the others stay silent; and in the United States it is not the practice for a guilty wife to clamor for the rights of women while she tramples on her holiest duties.

It has often been remarked that in Europe a certain contempt lurks even in the flattery men lavish on women. A European often pretends to be woman’s slave, yet it can be seen that he never sincerely thinks her his equal. In the United States men seldom pay compliments to women, but every day they show how much they esteem them. They constantly display complete confidence in a wife’s understanding and deep respect for her freedom. They have decided that her mind is as fit as a man’s to discover plain truth, and her heart as firm in embracing it; and they have never tried to shelter her virtue, any more than his, behind prejudice, ignorance, and fear. In Europe, where man so easily submits to the despotic sway of women, it seems that women are nonetheless cut off from some of the greatest qualities of the human species and treated as seductive but imperfect beings. And, what may well provoke astonishment, women in the end see themselves in the same light, and almost regard it as a privilege that they are entitled to show themselves frivolous, feeble, and timid. The women of America claim no such privileges.

Again, it may be said that in our morals we have reserved strange immunities for man, so that there is, as it were, one virtue for his use and another to guide his partner, and that in the view of the public the very same act may be punished at one time as a crime and at another as merely a fault. The Americans do not know this unjust division of duties and rights; among them the seducer is as dishonored as his victim. It is true that the Americans rarely lavish on women the eager attentions commonly paid to them in Europe. But their conduct toward women always implies that they suppose them virtuous and refined. Such is their respect for the moral freedom of the sex that in a woman’s presence the most guarded language is used, lest her ear be offended by some expression. In America a young unmarried woman can undertake a long journey alone and without fear.

The legislators of the United States, who have softened almost all the penalties of criminal law, still make rape a capital offense, and public opinion punishes no crime with more unrelenting severity. This can be explained. The Americans can conceive of nothing more precious than a woman’s honor, and nothing that ought to be more respected than her independence, so they hold that no punishment is too severe for the man who takes them from her against her will. In France, where the same offense is punished with far milder penalties, it is often difficult to get a jury to convict the accused. Does this come from contempt for decency or contempt for women? I cannot help believing that it is contempt for both.

Thus the Americans do not think that man and woman have either the duty or the right to perform the same functions, but they show equal regard for both of their respective parts; and though their lot is different, they consider them beings of equal worth. They do not give woman’s courage the same form or direction as man’s, but they never doubt her courage. And if they hold that man and his partner ought not always to use their intellect and understanding in the same way, they at least believe that the understanding of the one is as sound as that of the other, and her intellect as clear. So, while they have allowed the social inferiority of woman to continue, they have done all they could to raise her morally and intellectually to the level of man. In this respect they seem to me to have understood admirably the true principle of democratic improvement. As for myself, I do not hesitate to declare that although the women of the United States are confined within the narrow circle of domestic life, and their situation is in some respects one of extreme dependence, I have nowhere seen woman hold a loftier position. And if I were asked, now that I am drawing near the close of this work, in which I have spoken of so many important things done by the Americans, to what the singular prosperity and growing strength of that people should chiefly be attributed, I would answer: to the superiority of their women.
